title: Who can see the club file?
objective: Identify what needs protecting and explain how three different problems can affect the same file.

warmup.title: Three ways to ruin a pizza order
warmup.text: Your class has one shared pizza order form. In one minute, list three different ways the order could go wrong before lunch. Keep your list. You will sort it later.

terms.meaning: Protecting computers, accounts and digital information so people can use them safely.
Something people rely on and want to protect, such as a club's schedule.
Approval to do a particular thing with a particular resource.
Only people with permission can see the information.
Information stays accurate and changes happen as intended.
People with permission can use the information when they need it.

example: The cafeteria menu screen works, but yesterday's lunch is still listed. I would check the date against today's menu because a working screen can still give people the wrong information.
caseText: The Harbor School art club needs its setup sheet for Friday's show. You have permission to examine the fictional cards below. At the show, even a sheet with every name spelled correctly can let the crew down.
evidence: Club agreement. Only crew members and the adviser may read the setup sheet. Only the adviser may edit it. The crew needs it at 2 p.m. on Friday.

At rehearsal, a crew member and a visitor both see “Connected to school Wi-Fi.” Both can read the public show program. The original setup sheet opens for the crew member. The visitor sees “You need permission.”
Copy A. The guesses for surprise award winners are on the sheet. Anyone at school can read it. All entries still match the adviser's copy.
Copy B. Only the crew and adviser can open it. The adviser confirmed the crew meets in Room 12, but the sheet now says Room 21.
Copy C. The saved entries match the adviser's copy. At 2 p.m. the crew's screen says “File unavailable.”
tasks: Name the file the club is protecting. At rehearsal, which result shows both people have a working network connection? Which result shows their file permissions differ? Decide whether the visitor's message matches the club agreement.
For A, B, and C, identify the main security concern. Underline one clue on each card. Tell a partner how the problem would affect someone at the show.
Pick one copy. Recommend a change the adviser could make, then describe what a crew member or adviser would observe if it worked.
exit: At 2 p.m. the crew can open the supply list, and only crew members can read it. It says to bring 4 tables. The adviser approved 14. Which security goal needs attention? Give the clue that decided it.

teacher.instruction: Run the pizza-order warm-up. Collect the ways the order could go wrong in students’ own words and keep the list on the board for sorting by security goal later.

Compare the two rehearsal results on paper. Ask which clue describes the Wi-Fi connection and which describes access to the file. Then relate each security goal to who can read the sheet, its accuracy or the time it is needed. Sort the warm-up list under the three goals.
Give pairs the three copy cards. Have one reader name the effect on the crew and the other locate evidence. Switch roles after each card.
Pairs trade one proposed change and test. Ask whether the test checks the original problem and respects the club agreement.
Give the exit case individually. Collect the chosen security goal and the numerical clue.

lookFor: Students justify each goal with a detail from the file and connect the proposed fix to the people affected.
support: Read one copy at a time. Ask yourself who can see it, whether it is correct and whether the crew can get it on time. Point to a clue and explain it aloud.
stretch: The adviser locks the sheet so only the adviser can open it. Which original problem might that solve? What new problem would the crew have on Friday?

title: Give each person the access they need
objective: Design an account and sharing plan that protects a club roster while letting people do their jobs.

warmup.title: Passphrase showdown
warmup.text: Rank these three invented sign-in secrets from easiest to hardest to guess: soccer12, S0cc3r!2 and lantern-pickle-orbit-canoe. Be ready to say why. Never use a worksheet example as a real password.

terms.meaning: A long password made from several words. Choose unrelated words privately and use a different passphrase for each account.
A sign-in check that uses two different kinds of proof, such as a passphrase you know and a security key you have.
Give a person just the access they need for their job, for the time they need it.

example: A stage manager updates the rehearsal calendar. As an actor, I only need to read it to find my rehearsal, so I would ask for viewing access.
caseText: The art club co-chairs need Friday's roster. The yearbook editor asks how many students joined. Sketch a sharing plan on paper. Keep every real passphrase, code and account detail out of your work.
evidence: The roster has 18 member names, the jobs they picked and an attendance column. The two co-chairs update attendance using school accounts. The adviser manages sharing.
The yearbook editor needs one number for a caption. Club members need the list of available jobs but can choose a job by telling a co-chair.
Plan A. Both co-chairs share one sign-in. Its password is also used for a game. Anyone with the roster link can edit.
Plan B. Each co-chair has a separate school account with its own long passphrase and a school-issued security key for sign-in. The adviser can choose who gets the roster, a job list or a count.
tasks: Pick one risk in Plan A. What could happen if the game password became public, or if a roster link reached the wrong person? Match your risk to one safeguard in Plan B and explain how it would help.
Make a four-row list for adviser, co-chair, member and yearbook editor. Write what each role receives and what that person may do. Account for the caption and the attendance update.
A co-chair steps down. Circle the permissions the adviser should review. Sketch a check showing that the new co-chair can do the job and the former co-chair can no longer edit.
exit: A member signs in with a passphrase and security key. The roster then lets them edit attendance by mistake. Which setting should the adviser review, and why did the sign-in checks still succeed?

teacher.instruction: Run the passphrase showdown and ask why four unrelated words beat a short word with swapped symbols. Then read the yearbook request and ask students to answer it in the fewest pieces of information possible.
Draw two boxes. Label one “Who signed in?” and the other “What may they do?” Model where a security key and an edit setting fit.
Pairs draw a line from their chosen risk in Plan A to a safeguard in Plan B and explain the match. Then they build the four-row sharing list and check that each permission serves a job.
Announce the change in co-chairs. Partners revise their lists and explain how the adviser could check both roles using the school's approved process.
Students complete the exit individually using the two questions from the board.

lookFor: Each role can finish its assigned job. The explanation distinguishes signing in from the actions someone can take afterward.
support: Make a table with the headings Person, Job, Information and Allowed action. You can also say your choices aloud or arrange role cards with a partner.
stretch: A new volunteer needs to check people in for one meeting. Design access that ends after the job and a way to confirm when it has ended.

activity.label: Practice safe security habits
activity.prompt: Open the Explore, Practice and Check tabs. Add a second sign-in factor to the practice account and limit what it may do. Record which step proved who was signing in and which step limited their actions. Use only the practice account on the screen.

title: Follow a message across the network
objective: Trace a web page request step by step and explain which part of the trip HTTPS protects.

warmup.title: Packet relay
warmup.text: Write a twelve-word message. Tear it into four strips and number them. Pass each strip across the room by a different route. Can the reader rebuild it? What should the reader do if strip 3 never arrives?

terms.meaning: A small, numbered chunk of data. Large messages travel as many packets and are put back together at the other end.
The number that identifies a device’s connection on a network, so packets know where to go.
A device that passes packets from one network toward another.
The internet’s contact list. It finds the IP address that belongs to a name.
A way of loading a web page that encrypts what travels between your browser and the site and checks the site’s certificate for that name.

example: I type the library’s web address. Before anything loads, my browser asks DNS for the number that goes with that name, the way I look up a contact before I call.
caseTitle: The stream that would not load
caseText: Families want to watch the Harbor School robotics club demo on the club page. It loads for some people and fails for others. You are the club’s network tracker. Every name and address on these cards is invented.
evidence: Trip cards, shuffled. (P) The browser checks the site’s certificate and sets up an encrypted HTTPS connection. (Q) The laptop joins the school Wi-Fi and is given a local address, 10.20.4.37. (R) The web server at 203.0.113.20 sends the page back as packets. (S) The browser asks a DNS server which address belongs to clubs.harbor.example. (T) The browser puts the packets back in order and shows the page.
Always on duty. Routers pass each packet along, one hop at a time, toward the address written on it. Every step after the laptop joins the network depends on them.
Report 1. A tablet in the gym shows no Wi-Fi bars. The laptop beside it loads the club page.
Report 2. On one laptop, typing clubs.harbor.example gives “Server not found.” From the same laptop, the adviser’s connection test to 203.0.113.20 succeeds.
Report 3. On the bus Wi-Fi, a sign-in page opens at an address starting http:// and the browser shows “Not secure.”
Wi-Fi card. The club poster says the school network is named HarborSchool and asks for a school sign-in. At the game, a second network named HarborSchool-FREE appears and asks for nothing.
tasks: Put trip cards P to T in order. Star the card where a name becomes a number. Draw a lock on the card where the data gets scrambled for the trip.
Match each report to the trip card where the trouble starts. Quote the clue that told you. For one report, say what you would test next and what result would prove you right.

Mark each statement true or false, then fix the false ones. “The lock icon means the people running the site are honest.” “HTTPS keeps others on the same Wi-Fi from reading what I send to the site.” “Two networks with nearly the same name must belong to the same owner.” Decide what to do about the Wi-Fi card and who to ask.
exit: A classmate says, “The page has a lock, so the message asking for my password must be real.” What does the lock tell you? What does it leave out?

teacher.instruction: Run the packet relay with one volunteer message. Ask how the numbers helped and what the reader should request when a strip goes missing.
Introduce the five terms with the worked example. Model the first two trip cards on the board and place the router card beside the whole route.
Pairs order the remaining trip cards and match the three reports. One partner names the step and the other finds the clue. Ask each pair for a test that would confirm one diagnosis.
Work the three lock statements and the Wi-Fi card. Pairs that finish early can open the beginner networking lab and compare its name-lookup card with report 2.
Give the lock exit individually. Collect what HTTPS protects and what it cannot promise.

lookFor: Students place the name lookup before the secure connection and tie each report to a specific step with a quoted clue. They separate an encrypted connection from a trustworthy sender.
support: Act it out. One person is the browser, one is DNS and one is the web server. Hand the trip cards along in order and say what each person does.
stretch: Three packets arrive in the order 2, 3, 1. Explain how the numbers fix that. Then decide what the receiver should ask for when packet 2 never arrives.

activity.label: Follow a network connection
activity.prompt: Open the Explore, Practice and Check tabs. Connect the practice PC, let it get its network settings and open the practice page. Find the name lookup card and compare it with report 2. Record one part that carried the connection and one that only looked up a name.

title: Keep a secret, catch a change
objective: Use a shift cipher to see how a key protects a message, then use a fingerprint to tell whether a file was changed.

warmup.title: KHOOR
warmup.text: Every letter in KHOOR was moved three places forward in the alphabet. Move each one back three. What does it say? Time yourself.

terms.meaning: Scrambling information so that only someone with the right key can read it.
The secret piece of information that locks and unlocks an encrypted message.
The method used to scramble a message. A shift cipher moves every letter the same number of places.
Trying every possible key until one works.
A short fingerprint calculated from a file. Change the file and the fingerprint changes too.

example: My key is 4, so C becomes G, L becomes P, U becomes Y and B becomes F. I send GPYF. My partner knows the key, counts back four and reads CLUB.
caseText: The Harbor School puzzle club hides the start of its scavenger hunt in a scrambled note. A copy of the hunt rules is also going around, and one copy looks different. You are the club’s code cracker. Everything on these cards is invented.
evidence: Note found by locker 114. “AOL OBUA ZAHYAZ HA AOL NFT KVVY”
Club cipher card. Every letter moved forward the same number of places, wrapping from Z back to A. That number is the key. A shift cipher has only 25 keys that change the message.
Real-world card. The encryption that protects a web page uses a key picked from more possibilities than every computer on Earth could try in billions of years.

Fingerprint card. The adviser posted the rule START AT NOON with fingerprint 157. The club fingerprint adds the position of every letter, so A adds 1 and Z adds 26. The hallway copy of the rule says START AT NINE.
tasks: Decode the worked example’s GPYF yourself to check the method. Then look at the locker note. One three-letter word appears twice. Use it to guess the key.
A partner chooses a key and whispers it to you. Scramble a three-word invented reply and trade. Explain why the key must travel by a different route from the note.
Fingerprint the hallway copy. Compare it with the adviser’s number. Say what the fingerprint proves and what it cannot tell you about who changed the rule.

courseLab.title: Crack the Locker Note
courseLab.introduction: You moved four letters by hand. Now turn a cipher wheel to crack the whole locker note, send a secret reply and catch the copy of the rules that changed.
steps: Turn the wheel until the note reads as English. Record the key and how many keys you tried.
Scramble a short invented reply and choose how the key should reach your partner.
Fingerprint both copies of the rule. Decide which copy still matches the adviser’s and what the fingerprint cannot tell you.
courseLab.artifact: Hand in the key, your count of tries and both fingerprints. Add one sentence on why real encryption cannot be cracked the way you cracked the note.

exit: Encryption and hashing do different jobs. Which one keeps a note secret? Which one shows that a download was changed? Match each to a security goal from lesson 1.

teacher.instruction: Race the KHOOR warm-up. Ask what a reader must know to undo the scramble and name that piece the key.
Introduce the terms with the worked example. Model moving one word by a key of 4 and back again. Ask how many different keys a shift cipher can have.
Give each pair Crack the Locker Note in its browser or paper edition. One partner turns the wheel while the other tallies keys tried. Swap roles for the reply and the fingerprint check.
Draw two columns headed Keeps it secret and Shows it changed. Sort the note, the key, the fingerprint and the hallway copy. Ask why the fingerprint cannot name a person.
Give the exit individually. Collect one job for encryption, one for hashing and the matching security goals.

lookFor: Students find the key by reasoning from a repeated word or by an organized brute-force search. They explain that the key must stay private, and they separate keeping a message secret from detecting a change.
support: Write the alphabet on two paper strips. Slide the bottom strip to line up a guess, then read straight across. Try the shortest words first.
stretch: TAB and BAT have the same club fingerprint. Explain why. Then explain why the fingerprints used for real downloads are designed so that nobody can find two files that match.

title: Decide what to do with an urgent message
objective: Use a message's request, destination and context to decide whether to report it, verify it or use a known route.

warmup.title: Hold the door?
warmup.text: A stranger carrying a huge box asks you to hold open the locked computer lab door. Thumbs up, thumbs down or “ask first”? Be ready to say what you would check, and how.

terms.meaning: Tricking a person into opening the door, instead of breaking the lock. It works on computers, phones and real doors.
A deceptive message that tries to get someone to reveal information or take a harmful action.
The label shown beside a message. Two senders can use the same label.
Check a request through a route you already trust, such as talking to the adviser in person.

example: A message tells me my library book is overdue. I can check the due date in the library app I already use, even if I have no idea who sent the reminder.
caseText: It's ten minutes before club. Three notes arrive at once. Read the paper message cards or practice inspecting clues in Inbox Defender. All the requests below are fictional.
evidence: Message A. Display name “Art Club Help.” It asks for a sign-in code in a reply within two minutes to save the roster. You did not start a sign-in. The class help poster says to take unexpected code requests to the adviser.

Message B. A familiar classmate's name appears on an unexpected invitation to review a new poster folder. It asks for no secret. You can ask the classmate at the meeting before opening the invitation.
Message C. This morning the adviser said a supply checklist would appear in the class portal. A reminder asks you to use your usual portal bookmark. It includes no link and requests no reply.
tasks: For each card choose an action. Use “stop and report,” “verify another way,” or “use the known bookmark.” Name the exact detail that influenced you most.
Write the first sentence you would say to the adviser about A. Include what the message asked for and whether you took any action. Keep secrets out of your report.
A partner says B must be safe because the name looks familiar. Give a reason for checking and identify one way to do so without using the invitation.
exit: A message labeled “Club Adviser” says the room changed and asks you to use an unfamiliar link for directions. You can see the adviser across the hall. What will you do first, and what makes that check independent?

teacher.instruction: Take the hold-the-door vote and name the trick: asking a helpful person to skip a check. Then read only the display names on the paper messages. Invite predictions, reveal the actual requests and ask who wants more evidence.
Model locating a request, its destination and something the class already knows. Introduce the three response options.
Use Inbox Defender's Evidence challenge in pairs or read the three cards aloud. Each pair records a decision and two clues for one case.
Use all three paper cases for comparison. Partners write a short report for A and rehearse an independent check for B. Ask one pair to justify handling C differently.
Collect an individual decision and a reason for the exit scenario.

lookFor: The decision for each message cites its particular request and a clue about where it came from, where it leads or what the club already knows.
support: Ask a partner to read one message at a time. Point to an action in the first task, then quote or describe the clue you used.
stretch: Rewrite the reminder in C after the adviser changes the plan to tomorrow. Which facts would a reader be able to confirm independently? Then explain why perfect spelling no longer proves a message is real, now that AI tools can polish any message.

activity.label: Play Inbox Defender
activity.prompt: Choose Evidence challenge. In a round, inspect the sender, destination and context before choosing a response. Record two clues and explain your decision. The three message cards work on paper.

title: Build your layers
objective: Match safeguards to the ways a small computer lab can fail and design layers that still hold when one of them breaks.

warmup.title: Swiss cheese stack
warmup.text: Punch three holes in each of three scrap sheets, in different places. Stack them. Can you see through? Now line the holes up. What would each sheet be if this stack were guarding a computer?

terms.meaning: A weakness that could be used to cause harm, such as software that is missing a fix.
Software made to harm, spy or lock files. Ransomware is malware that locks files and demands payment.
A fix from the software’s maker. Many updates close a known weakness, which is why waiting is risky.
A separate copy kept somewhere else, which you can restore if the original is lost.
Using several different safeguards, so one failure does not sink everything.

example: My bike has a lock, a registered serial number and a spot inside the garage. If I forget to lock it one day, the other two still help. No single layer has to be perfect.
caseText: The Cedar Middle media club is editing a documentary on three shared laptops. The adviser gives your team six shield points to spend on safeguards. Spend them where they matter. The lab and its troubles are invented.
evidence: Lab facts. Three laptops stay in an unlocked room. Every member signs in with the same administrator account. The only copy of the documentary is on laptop 2.
Trouble card 1. A free “video speed booster” download asks for the administrator password before it will install.
Trouble card 2. Laptop 3 has postponed its updates for nine weeks. The maker released a fix for a known weakness in week one.
Trouble card 3. A drink spills on laptop 2 the night before the premiere. Nobody attacked anything.
Trouble card 4. A laptop is missing from the unlocked room on Monday morning.

Safeguard menu. Automatic updates, 1 point. Weekly backup to the school drive, 2 points. Second backup kept in another building, 2 points. Locked cabinet, 1 point. Separate member accounts without install rights, 1 point. Club rule to install only from the school’s approved list, 1 point. School security software that scans downloads, 1 point. “Hackers keep out” sticker, 1 point.
tasks: For each trouble card, name the weakness that let it happen and every safeguard on the menu that would help. Label each safeguard as technology, a rule for people or a physical barrier.
Spend exactly six points. Draw your layers as rings around the documentary. Pick one trouble card and show two different layers that cover it.

Stress test. Your partner picks a trouble card and crosses out one of your layers, saying “that one failed today.” Does another layer still catch the trouble? Revise your plan and say what you gave up.
exit: The club’s only backup sits in a folder on laptop 2, beside the documentary. Name one event that would destroy both copies. Where should a better backup live?

teacher.instruction: Run the Swiss cheese stack. Ask what happens when every hole lines up, and why three different sheets beat three copies of the same sheet.
Introduce the terms. Read the lab facts and trouble cards aloud. Ask which trouble involves no attacker at all, and why it still counts as a security problem.
Pairs match troubles to safeguards, label each one as technology, rule or physical, then spend six points and draw their rings.
Run the stress test. Each partner removes one layer and plays one trouble card. Pairs revise and report one trade-off they accepted.
Give the backup exit individually. Collect the shared failure and a better location.

lookFor: Students connect each safeguard to a specific weakness, mix technology, rules and physical barriers, and can show a second layer catching a trouble after the first one fails. They notice that the sticker protects nothing.
support: Lay the four trouble cards in a row. Under each one, place every safeguard that would have helped. Start spending on the trouble with the fewest cards under it.
stretch: A common backup rule is 3-2-1: keep three copies, on two kinds of storage, with one copy somewhere else. Score the club’s current setup against that rule and say what one more point would buy.

title: Rebuild a timeline and check the recovery
objective: Use time-stamped records to report a fictional incident, identify what is still unknown and check a proposed recovery.

warmup.title: Seen or guessed?
warmup.text: A classmate reports, “The lab door was open at 8:05. The projector was warm. Someone watched a movie before school.” Which parts did somebody observe? Which part is a guess?

terms.meaning: A record of events that includes times and observations.
An action that limits further harm while someone investigates.
Restoring the work people need and checking that they can use it again.

example: After a morning announcement cuts out, the technician says the microphone has power again. I would ask someone at the back of the gym whether they can hear a whole sentence.
caseText: Friday's art show needs 12 printed display labels. The adviser keeps old versions of the label sheet. You are the student who found a problem. Use the records to give the adviser an accurate handoff.
evidence: 1:24 p.m. • Adviser's test. A member opens the restored copy and counts 12 labels. Print preview shows only 8.
1:04 p.m. • Adviser's note. The approved sheet has 12 finished labels. The adviser saves a copy marked 1:04.
1:16 p.m. • Adviser's note. Editing is paused. The adviser keeps the changed sheet and its history, then opens a separate copy of the 1:04 version.
1:12 p.m. • Member report. The sheet opens, but 4 of the 12 label rows are blank. No one saw how the rows changed.
tasks: Order the four records by time. In two sentences report what the member actually observed and one fact the records cannot tell the adviser.
Mark one action that limits further changes and one that preserves evidence. Explain why the adviser would keep the changed sheet while working on a separate copy.

Use the timeline to finish the club's response playbook, a short guide to what to do next. Fill in both lines for the adviser. “If the print test falls short, we should ___.” “We can tell the crew the labels are ready when ___.” Use the 1:24 record to decide which line applies now.

courseLab.title: The Double-Counted Ballot
courseLab.introduction: The art crew needed to know whether all 12 labels would print. Now the art club needs to know whether its results board counted each ballot once.
steps: Read the preliminary totals and the signed club rule. Write down the displayed totals and explain what counts as one ballot.
Find a receipt that appears more than once. Test what happens when you count each receipt once. What changed on the board?
Choose what the crew can announce. Use one record to support it and identify one question a person still needs to check.
courseLab.artifact: Give the adviser a two-line handoff with the checked tally and its evidence on the first line. On the second, say what remains unknown and who should check it.

exit: A copy of the seating chart opens after recovery. The door team still gets “Access denied.” Write the next handoff in two lines. What has been verified, and what does the team still need someone to test?

teacher.instruction: Use the warm-up to separate what was observed from a guess. Then ask what the print-table crew needs in its hands at showtime and write its success condition on the board.
As a class, order the art-show records and circle the action that preserved the changed sheet. Use the 1:24 print result to finish the two playbook lines together. Ask what nobody saw happen.

Give each pair The Double-Counted Ballot in its browser or paper edition. One partner reads the signed counting rule while the other compares the display with the receipt ledger. Swap roles to test a count-once rule and write the evidence and open question in a handoff.
Have two pairs exchange handoffs. Can the readers find the record behind the announced result? Ask them to underline any claim about a person that the records cannot establish.
Give the seating-chart exit. Ask each learner to use the same two-line handoff to distinguish tested access from access still needing a check.

lookFor: In the art case, students name a time and an observation and check the print result before declaring recovery. In the ballot handoff, they support the tally with a receipt and leave the cause open.
support: Arrange the four records by time or ask a partner to read them aloud. Start your report with “At ___ we saw ___” and “We still need to check ___.”
stretch: The 1:04 copy omitted a new label approved at 1:08. What additional evidence would the adviser need before choosing a final version?

title: Hackers with permission
objective: Use a testing agreement to decide which actions are allowed, report a weakness responsibly and match security jobs to the skills you have practiced.

warmup.title: Locksmith or burglar?
warmup.text: A locksmith and a burglar can open the same lock with the same tools. List three things that make one of them a professional and the other a criminal.

terms.meaning: Clear permission from the owner of a system to test it.
The exact systems, actions and times that the permission covers. Everything else is off limits.
A security professional who looks for weaknesses with permission, so that they can be fixed. Also called a penetration tester.
Reporting a weakness privately to the people who can fix it, without using it or spreading it.
A person or group that might cause harm. Their reasons differ, from money to showing off.

example: I notice the gym storage door does not latch. I do not go in to see what I could take. I tell the coach which door, when I noticed and that I left it alone.
caseTitle: The bug in the lunch app
caseText: The Harbor School coding club built a lunch pre-order app and keeps a practice copy for testing. Rey, a club member, has stumbled on a weakness in the live app. Help Rey decide what happens next. The app, the orders and the people are invented.
evidence: What Rey saw. Rey’s order page address ends in order=118. Rey mistyped 119 and another student’s sandwich order appeared. Rey closed the page.

Testing agreement, signed by the adviser. Club members may test the practice copy at practice.lunch.harbor.example during club meetings, using test accounts only. Report every weakness to the adviser the same day. The live app and real orders are outside this agreement.

Four ideas from classmates. (1) “Try every number from 1 to 500 on the live app to see how bad it is.” (2) “Post a screenshot in the group chat to warn everyone.” (3) “Tell the adviser today. Say what you typed, what appeared and that you stopped.” (4) “Stay quiet so you do not get in trouble.”

Career cards. Security operations analyst: watches alerts and investigates. Penetration tester: tests systems with written permission. Incident responder: contains a problem and helps people recover. Security awareness trainer: teaches people to spot tricks. AI security tester: checks whether AI tools can be fooled. Policy and compliance analyst: writes the rules and checks they are followed.
tasks: Sort the four ideas into inside the agreement, outside the agreement or leaves the weakness unfixed. For each, quote the line of the agreement or the fact from Rey’s card that decided it.
Write Rey’s report to the adviser in three sentences. Include what Rey typed, what appeared, when it happened and that Rey stopped. Leave out the other student’s name and order.
Pick two career cards. For each, name a lesson in this course where you did part of that job. Write one question you would ask a person who does it for a living.
exit: A friend says, “I only looked. I did not change anything.” Use the words authorization and scope to explain why looking can still break the rules.

teacher.instruction: Collect answers to the locksmith warm-up. Group them under permission, purpose and what happens to what they find.

Introduce the terms. Read the testing agreement together and box three limits: which copy, when and which accounts. Note that entering systems or accounts without permission can break school rules and the law.
Pairs sort the four ideas and write Rey’s three-sentence report. Ask why the report leaves out the other student’s details.
Hand out the career cards. Pairs match two jobs to earlier lessons and share one question for a professional. Point out that every job on the cards works with permission.
Give the exit individually. Collect an explanation that uses both authorization and scope.

lookFor: Students use the agreement’s own words to rule actions in or out, report the weakness without exposing another student, and recognize that skill without permission is not ethical hacking.
support: Underline three limits in the agreement: where, when and with which accounts. Hold each classmate idea against those three limits, one at a time.
stretch: Write two more lines for the testing agreement: one that covers what a tester does after seeing real data by accident, and one that says how fast the club must fix a reported weakness.
